reasoning: Both outputs break the search fixation and both use an explicit generative method, so the decision turns on the two things the eval flags as sharpest: honest structural distinctness of the candidate set, and whether the fixation itself gets diagnosed. B wins both. On distinctness: A presents 20 ideas, but only ~10 are genuinely distinct mechanisms — chronological/visual browse appears in five costumes (#1 recents-as-home, #4 resume strip, #7 photo library, #15 time-and-context index, #17 time machine, and #20's skeuomorph pick is the same photo library again), and #16 monthly digest is a subset of #13 proactive resurfacing. That is a ~50% duplication rate in the headline list, the exact 'tags/folders/collections in three costumes' failure the eval penalizes. A does mitigate it honestly by clustering down to 7 candidates (A-G) that ARE all structurally distinct, so the set it actually recommends on is clean — but the reader has to wade through the padding to get there. B presents 13 and ~10 are genuinely distinct: the only real collapses are #5 episodic grouping / #6 time-bucket browse (one mechanism, two costumes), #7 visible facets sitting close to #6, and #11 cross-bucket index / #12 self-serve restore being two halves of one dead-end-elimination mechanism (B itself bundles them into Approach B). Roughly 77% density against A's 50%. B also bucket-labels its candidates by mechanism family (prevent the loss / make recognizable / reach the tail / remove the task / kill the dead end), which makes distinctness checkable rather than asserted. Mechanism span is close to even — A uniquely has the reframe-the-job family (re-use over retrieve, portfolio view, share-history as a retrieval channel), B uniquely has existence/policy ('nothing disappears silently'), the spatial no-list option, and failure mode 6, 'Belief — nobody searches for what they've mourned,' which is the single most original observation in either document. On the fixation: this is decisive. The user said 'I can't get past it.' B opens with four named cognitive mechanisms for why THIS person keeps landing on search — inheriting the user's own solution-hypothesis wholesale because the ticket's verb is 'find'; availability (every tool has a search box, so it crowds the slot); search converts mushy ambiguity into something buildable and estimable by Friday, which is relief from not knowing; and it is the lowest-blame option, 'an option that can't be wrong also can't be evaluated' — plus the tell that 'a support ticket means the user already tried,' so search's likely effect is converting 'I can't find it' into the worse ticket 'I searched and it's not there.' A's Part 1 explains why the IDEA is insufficient (correct, not differentiating, mis-sequenced) and validates the instinct, which is good, but it never diagnoses why the person is stuck. That is the difference between 'here is what's wrong with your idea' and 'here is why your head keeps going there.' Generative method is close to a tie: A runs 20 named angles across 5 families (constraint manipulation, structural, psychology, perspective shift, experience design) — broader and more explicitly labeled; B runs four passes (word-by-word deconstruction of the complaint sentence, six failure modes, a create-name-store-resurface-retrieve-recover lifecycle map showing 'search occupies exactly one cell of six', and inversion) — tighter and better fitted, and the lifecycle map is the sharpest single generative move in either doc. A's forced-angle approach is precisely what produces its near-duplicates. A is genuinely strong and beats B in places: its stress test is richer (survivorship bias in the ticket corpus; 'top support complaint is a weaker signal than it feels' because it may just be the easiest complaint to articulate; auto-naming can be worse than 'Untitled' because a confidently wrong name makes every row demand evaluation), and its evaluation apparatus is more complete (value/usability/feasibility/viability per candidate, Differentiator/MMR/Quick-Win/Dud classification, risk-impact 2x2, a named validation move per candidate, and metrics with a failure canary and a counter-metric). B's cost is scope drift: section 5 is an architecture spec for one approach, which the prompt ('need better options') did not ask for, and the document deliberately ends incomplete pending approval. But B's own sharp additions offset that — the metric choice in particular ('not ticket volume; ticket volume falls when people give up' -> dormant-project reopen rate) is better reasoned than A's primary metric, and the security note that a stale unified index leaking another account's project title is worse than the original bug is a real catch. Net: A is the better-packaged option menu; B is the better answer to the question actually asked, because the user's stated blocker was the fixation and only B takes it apart.

A's final clustered set of 7 is immaculate and its mechanism span is marginally wider on the reframe-the-job axis, but the headline list of 20 is half costume-changes — the specific failure the eval penalizes.

fixation_analysis.A: Explains why the IDEA is insufficient, not why the USER is stuck. Part 1 gives three properties of search (correct, not differentiating, mis-sequenced) and validates the instinct — 'the instinct that it's lazy is a real signal, keep it.' The strongest line, 'search is a query language for people who already remember the answer; it asks the user to supply a name at the exact moment when name-recall is what failed,' is a critique of the mechanism, not a diagnosis of the fixation. The user said 'I can't get past it' and A does not tell them why.
fixation_analysis.B: Directly diagnoses the fixation with four named mechanisms: inheriting the ticket's own verb and therefore the user's solution-hypothesis; availability (search is the most retrievable exemplar of 'helping people locate things' and crowds the slot); it converts unbounded ambiguity into a ticket that's estimable by Friday, so reaching for it is partly relief from not knowing; and it is the lowest-blame option — 'an option that can't be wrong also can't be evaluated, which is exactly why it stays.' Adds the tell that a support ticket means the user already tried the obvious, so search most likely converts the complaint into a worse one.
fixation_analysis.verdict: B, clearly. This is the expectation the prompt most explicitly asked for and only B answers it.
